project.name: Existence of the q-colorability threshold for sparse random graphs
project.description: For every integer q at least 3, the formalization proves the existence of a limiting q-colorability threshold for sparse random graphs. A single constant alpha_q in [1/2, log(q)/log(q/(q-1))] gives the transition for the uniform model with floor(c n) edges and the transition at d = 2 alpha_q for the binomial model with edge probability d/n. For every fixed eta in (0,1), there is C > 0 such that, for all sufficiently large n, the first loss of q-colorability under independent uniform additions of unordered pairs of distinct vertices lies within C n (log n)^(-3/2) steps of deterministic integer centers with probability at least 1-eta. The centers divided by n converge to the same alpha_q. Repeated edges are retained in this process. The scope is Theorems 1.1 and 1.2 of the included manuscript.

status.scope: The two headline theorems, combined under one existential threshold in ThresholdChallenge.MainStatement. The project does not claim a separate formalization of every remark, literature statement, or consequence in the manuscript, does not identify the numerical value of the threshold, and asserts no conclusion at the threshold itself.

fidelity.divergences: Vertices and colors use Fin n and Fin q in place of the manuscript's one-based finite sets. The uniform simple-graph probability is represented by exact finite counts, the binomial probability by its finite Bernoulli sum, and process probabilities by counts of ordered edge prefixes sampled with replacement. The binomial d/n probability is set to zero outside 0 < n and 0 <= d <= n; for every fixed d >= 0, this affects only finitely many n. Natural floor is used at nonnegative c n. Window centers are integers, the logarithm exponent is the real number -3/2, and the onset is strengthened harmlessly to n_0 >= max(3, 2q). One existential threshold is shared by the threshold and window statements. No definition holes or additional literature axioms are used. The sole sorry in Challenge.lean is the deliberate Comparator challenge placeholder, not an unresolved proof.
